Order Regarding 109 Response to Order to Show Cause. After over two months and multiple requests for extensions, Plaintiff's counsel has failed to fully comply with the Order to Show Cause. See ECF Nos. 66, 95. Plaintiff's counsel, Mr. Shahian, is ordered to cure his non-compliance by filing a supplemental declaration by July 10, 2026, by addressing the following deficiencies: (1) Mr. Shahian was specifically ordered to file a chart that includes "all instances in the last five years of when a court, either state or federal, sanctioned any attorney for conduct that occurred during the time that attorney worked for SLP." Mr. Shahian must include in his chart all instances of sanctions by SLP attorneys in the last five years.  1                                          INTRODUCTION
 2          Plaintiff Santiago Talavera Castro respectfully submits this Ex Parte Application for a 15-
 3   Day Extension of Time pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 6(b). This application is
 4   made in good faith and in furtherance of Plaintiff’s desire to comply with the Court’s May 6,
 5   2026 Order Continuing Order to Show Cause, Dkt. No. 95 (the “Order”) as best he can, after
 6   proper due diligence. Plaintiff’s counsel Strategic Legal Practices, APC (“SLP”) and its
 7   founder/managing partner Payam Shahian (collectively, Plaintiff’s Counsel) understands the
 8   Court’s concerns and seeks only the time necessary to adequately address them.
 9          The Order directs Mr. Shahian to file an updated declaration under penalty of perjury
10   providing, among other things, a comprehensive accounting of every sanction imposed on any
11   attorney who has ever worked for SLP for the past five years—including details such as the date
12   of sanction, the issuing court, the amount, and whether the sanction was reportable to the State
13   Bar. Dkt. No. 95, at 1-2. The deadline for Mr. Shahian to file his updated response is June 22,
14   2026. Id.
15          Plaintiff’s Counsel is endeavoring to comply to that order as best able—an order that
16   Plaintiff’s Counsel understands to be motivated by the Court’s concern with wanting to ensure
17   that SLP’s clients are receiving proper attention. That concern, which arose in large part from
18   former SLP partner Tionna Carvalho’s off-the-cuff statements at the April 22, 2026 hearing,
19   understandably alarmed the Court. See Dkt. No. 66, at 3-6. SLP takes the Court’s concern
20   seriously and wants to provide the Court with a response that is accurate, verified, and completed
21   after careful review. As set forth below, good cause supports a brief, 15-day extension of the
22   June 22, 2026 deadline.
23                                           BACKGROUND
24          Both parties missed the Court’s March 18, 2026 pretrial deadline. Dkt. No. 66, at 1. The
25   Court subsequently issued show-cause orders and various sanctions. Dkt. No. 66. As relevant
27   here, the Court ordered Mr. Shahian, to file a declaration providing an accounting of all sanctions
28   imposed on any SLP attorney in the past five years and an explanation of steps taken to ensure


                                          3

      Case 5:24-cv-06274-NW            Document 106        Filed 06/22/26      Page 4 of 7




 1   SLP’s compliance with all rules (including the rules of professional responsibility, rules of court,
 2   and rules of procedure), laws, standing orders, case specific orders, and deadlines. Dkt. No. 95,
 3   at 1-2.
 4             Plaintiff’s Counsel appealed the order and sought a stay—first in this Court (Dkt. No.
 5   101), and then in the Ninth Circuit (Case No. 26-3280, Dkt. Entry 11). Plaintiff’s Counsel was,
 6   inter alia, concerned that, although the Court seeks this information to protect consumers, the
 7   unintended impacts of the show-cause order would be to undermine Plaintiff’s Counsel’s clients’
 8   rights, and further, that FCA (and other manufacturers) would use any such filing to harm SLP’s
 9   consumer clients.
10             On Wednesday, June 17, 2026—just five days before the compliance deadline—FCA
11   filed an opposition to the stay in the Ninth Circuit, even though FCA is not implicated by the
12   show cause order directed solely to Plaintiff’s counsel. Case No. 26-3280, Dkt. Entry 13.1. In its
13   opposition, FCA confirmed that it is colluding with other manufacturers—its competitors—to
14   compile a list of all sanctions imposed in every imaginable case where SLP and/or SLP attorney
15   was sanctioned. Case No. 26-3280, Dkt. Entry 15.1, Sheridan Decl. ¶¶ 5-7 & Exs. A, B. That list
16   appears in two charts. See id.
17             The Ninth Circuit denied the emergency stay the following day, on June 18, 2026. Case
18   No. 26-3280, Dkt. Entry 19.1.
19             Plaintiff now seeks a 15-day extension of the June 22, 2026 deadline so that Mr. Shahian
20   and his ethics counsel have adequate time to review and verify FCA’s list and, as best able, to
21   provide the Court with an accurate accounting of the information it has requested.
22             This includes a detailed description of how SLP is run, including how its case load is
23   managed—so that Plaintiff’s Counsel can put the Court’s concerns to rest regarding the bases
24   that animated the show-cause orders in the first place. Indeed, Ms. Carvalho’s off-the-cuff
25   statements at the April 22, 2026 hearing do not provide a complete—and therefore do not
27   provide an accurate—picture of SLP or how it is handling cases. Simply put: Plaintiff’s Counsel
28   seek time to conduct the due diligence necessary to address the Court’s concerns.

 1                                             DISCUSSION
 2          Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 6(b) authorizes courts to extend deadlines for good
 3   cause. Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(b)(1)(A). The standard is “non-rigorous:” “[R]equests for extensions of
 4   time made before the applicable deadline has passed should ‘normally … be granted in the
 5   absence of bad faith on the part of the party seeking relief or prejudice to the adverse party.’”
 6   Ahanchian v. Xenon Pictures, Inc., 624 F.3d 1253, 1259 (9th Cir. 2010).
 7          There is no bad faith here. Plaintiff’s Counsel seeks additional time precisely because it
 8   wants to comply with the Court’s Order—and FCA will suffer no prejudice from a 15-day
 9   extension. The OSC hearing is not until July 14, 2026, and the extension would still leave FCA
10   and the Court ample time to review Mr. Shahian’s updated declaration before that hearing.
11          The most pressing basis for the extension is FCA’s June 17, 2026 filing in the Ninth
12   Circuit—submitted just days ago. In its opposition to the emergency stay, FCA disclosed that it
13   has been compiling a list of sanctions against SLP, in cooperation with other vehicle
14   manufacturers—its own competitors—to build a comprehensive list that it intends to supplement.
15   See Case No. 26-3280, Dkt. Entry 15.1, Sheridan Decl. ¶¶ 5–7 & Exs. A, B. Mr. Shahian and his
16   ethics counsel must now review this newly disclosed compilation to verify its accuracy,
17   determine which entries fall within the Court’s five-year lookback period, and incorporate any
18   confirmed sanctions into Mr. Shahian’s declaration. This is exactly the kind of “independent and
19   complete investigation” the Court has ordered Mr. Shahian to conduct. Dkt. No. 66, at 8.
20          Several additional factors support the requested extension.
21          First, many of the sanctions identified in FCA’s exhibits are not reportable to the State
22   Bar of California, see, e.g., Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 6068(o)(3) (sanctions under $1000 not
23   reportable), making them more difficult to locate and verify through SLP’s own records,
24   especially because of how SLP’s records are maintained, as explained below. Shahian Decl., ¶ 5.
25          Second, compiling the comprehensive chart the Court has requested—covering all
27   current and former attorneys over a five-year period—requires Mr. Shahian to conduct an
28   independent investigation beyond what SLP’s existing records readily provide. SLP maintains

 1   individual case files for each of its matters. SLP does not, however, maintain a single centralized
 2   database that records every sanction imposed—together with the issuing court, date, amount, and
 3   the specific attorney involved—across all current and former SLP attorneys for a five-year
 4   period. Shahian Decl., ¶ 6.
 5          Third, Mr. Shahian’s other professional commitments make compliance by June 22
 6   impracticable. This includes his role managing SLP’s affairs, his work on the prior stay motions,
 7   and in other cases such as Loria v. Kia (Case No. E085817), where he is defending a jury verdict
 8   and cross-appealing the trial court’s grant of nonsuit on civil penalties. The hard deadline for
 9   Plaintiff’s respondent’s brief and cross-appellant’s brief is July 2. Shahian Decl., ¶ 7.
10          Fourth, FCA—which itself missed the same March 18 deadline that triggered these
11   proceedings—should not be heard to complain about a 15-day extension that will only improve
12   the accuracy and completeness of SLP’s response to the Court’s Order. Shahian Decl., ¶ 8.
13          FCA suffers no legitimate prejudice from the extension.
14          Fifth, in contrast, Plaintiff’s Counsel will suffer substantial prejudice if the 15-day
15   extension request is denied. FCA and its fellow manufacturers have been assembling
16   ammunition in the form of every imaginable sanction SLP has ever received, including in cases
17   where SLP obtained objectively excellent results for its clients. See Shahian Decl., ¶ 9. And more
18   troubling, based on Mr. Shahian’s preliminary review, it appears that FCA has claimed the
19   existence of sanctions in cases where SLP was not even sanctioned.
20          For example, in Ashgyan v. General Motors, Case No. 24STCV08237, which settled for
21   $129,000, FCA ostensibly identified a $250 discovery sanction, but Plaintiff’s Counsel’s review
22   currently shows that no such sanction was issued. Shahian Decl., ¶ 9(a).
23          Likewise, in Galindo Cano v. General Motors, Case No. 30-2023-01320498, which
24   settled for $110,000, FCA ostensibly identified a $500 discovery sanction, but Plaintiff’s
25   Counsel’s review currently shows that no such sanction was issued. Shahian Decl., ¶ 9(b).
27          Indeed, not only does it appear that SLP was not sanctioned in these cases, but they also
28   resulted in very favorable settlements to SLP’s clients. See Shahian Decl., ¶ 9.

 1             Moreover, none of FCA’s actions in collusion with other manufacturers united front
 2   against SLP has anything to do with protecting consumers. Rather, those actions have everything
 3   to do with neutralizing an effective consumer advocate.
 4             Notably, FCA is among “the manufacturers with the highest number of lemons” and the
 5   “long[est] history of failing to comply with consumer protection and public safety laws.” Br. of
 6   Consumers for Auto Reliability and Safety as Amicus Curiae Supporting Pet., Niedermeier v.
 7   FCA US LLC, 15 Cal.5th 792 (2024) (No. S266034), 2021 WL 6423932, at *11-12. FCA is

 9   “FCA operates in open defiance of.” See Figueroa v. FCA US, LLC, 84 Cal. App. 5th 708, 714
10   (2022).
11             The fact that FCA and other manufacturers are apparently cooperating to compile
12   sanctions against one of the state’s leading consumer protection firms underscores the need for
13   Mr. Shahian to have the time to verify the accuracy of FCA’s list, consult with ethics counsel,
14   and ensure his declaration adequately responds to the Court’s concerns.
15                                              CONCLUSION

17   extension of the June 22, 2026 deadline—to July 7, 2026—for Mr. Shahian to file his updated
18   declaration in response to the Order. The OSC hearing is not scheduled until July 14, 2026, and
19   this brief extension will not prejudice any party. It will, however, provide SLP with the time to
20   conduct the due diligence necessary to prepare the response the Court has directed—one that
21   accounts for the sanctions information FCA and other manufacturers have only just disclosed. It
22   will also give Plaintiff’s Counsel the chance to put together a comprehensive description of how
23   SLP’s cases are managed, so that this Court can have a complete—and therefore accurate—
24   picture of SLP’s operations.

17          In considering Plaintiff’s Counsel’s motion for stay pending appeal, the

 1                  1.     Plaintiff’s Counsel Is Likely To Succeed on the Merits.
 2           In assessing the first Nken factor, Plaintiff’s Counsel can show that it will
 3    “more likely than not” succeed on the merits in overturning the penalties

 6                         a.     The scope of the sanctions contained within the Show
 7                                Cause Orders exceed the Court’s authority to issue

 9           Plaintiff’s Counsel will show that the Show-Cause Orders were effectively
10    unlawful injunctions seeking to manage the day-to-day practice of SLP, exceeding
11    the Court’s sanction authority, by requiring the firm to release trade secrets,
12    restricting its ability to dismiss unrelated civil actions, and requiring it to file
13    notices of settlement when such an agreement may only be reached if no such
14    notice is filed in the first place—thus prejudicing Plaintiff’s Counsel and hundreds
15    of nonparties in unrelated matters. See Nken, 556 U.S. at 434.
16           An injunction is a “means by which a court tells someone what to do or not
17    to.” Nken, 556 U.S. at 428. Under Article III and Congress’s granting of federal
18    court jurisdiction, the scope of an injunction is inherently limited. See, e.g., Trump
19    v. CASA, Inc., 606 U.S. 831, 861 (2025) (federal courts “resolve cases and
20    controversies consistent with the authority Congress has given them”); id. at 862–
21    63 (Thomas, J., concurring) (“As the Court recognizes, the complete-relief
22    principle operates as a ceiling: In no circumstance can a court award relief beyond
23    that necessary to redress the plaintiffs’ injuries.”); cf. Landis, 299 U.S. at 254–55
24    (court has inherent authority to control “causes on its docket” (emphasis added)).
25           “Sanctions imposed under Rule 37(b)(2) ‘must be specifically related to the
27    particular “claim” which was at issue in the order to provide discovery.’” Fjelstad
28    v. Am. Honda Motor Co., 762 F.2d 1334, 1342 (9th Cir. 1985). The Court cites no

 5          Both Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 16 and 37 (the provisions relied on by
 6    the Court) limit the scope of sanctions the Court can provide as those “just” and
 7    specifically relevant to the litigation. Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(f), 37(b). Under Rule

 9    from pretrial conferences. Rule 37(b) discovery sanctions are even more limited,
10    providing for specific sanctions commensurate with the nature of the violation
11    within the proceeding—i.e., specific facts being admitted, specific pleadings being
12    struck “in whole or in part,” or in drastic cases mandating dismissal of that specific
13    action. See Fjelstad, 762 F.2d at 1342; Gregory v. State of Montana, 118 F.4th
14    1069, 1076–77 (9th Cir. 2024) (abuse of discretion to rely on “inherent authority”
15    to issue sanctions in excess of “the requirements for imposing such sanctions under

18    were mostly rooted in the Court “control[ling] . . . its docket” under its inherent

20    the penalties on Plaintiff’s Counsel were disproportionate relative to defendant’s

25    Brands Holdings, Inc., 168 F.4th 608, 626 (9th Cir. 2026) (impermissible to

28    workplaces”).
